seoDescription: Learn to build production-ready Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) applications with reliable, high-quality results. This guide covers the full RAG lifecycle, from the basic stack of data ingestion and querying to overcoming common production blockers. Discover a tiered optimization framework, starting with tuning chunk sizes and metadata filters, moving to advanced retrieval like small-to-big, and exploring powerful techniques like multi-document agents and fine-tuning embeddings and LLMs for peak performance.

chapters.title: The First Step: How to Evaluate Your RAG System

chapters.title: A Tiered Approach to RAG Optimization

chapters.title: Table-Stakes #1: Tuning Chunk Size
chapters.description: This section explains the impact of tuning chunk size, noting that simply retrieving more tokens does not always lead to better performance due to issues like loss-in-the-middle.

chapters.title: Table-Stakes #2: Metadata Filtering
chapters.description: This chapter details how to use metadata filtering within a vector database to combine structured search with semantic search, significantly improving retrieval precision.

chapters.description: This final chapter covers the most advanced topic: fine-tuning both the embedding model for better retrieval and the LLM itself for improved synthesis and reasoning.

summary:
## The Challenge of Naive RAG

A basic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system often fails in production because of poor response quality. Key issues include:

- **Bad Retrieval**: The system fails to retrieve the correct context from the vector database.
  - **Low Precision**: The retrieved chunks are not all relevant, leading to hallucinations and the "lost in the middle" problem where the LLM ignores context buried in the prompt.
  - **Low Recall**: The necessary information to answer the query isn't retrieved at all.
- **LLM Weaknesses**: Language models themselves can produce hallucinations, irrelevant answers, or biased content.

## A Tiered Framework for Optimization

To move from a naive prototype to a production-ready system, use a tiered approach to optimization. Start with the simplest, highest-impact changes and progressively move to more complex techniques.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Before you start optimizing, you **must** have an evaluation framework in place. You need to define benchmarks and metrics to measure the performance of both the **retrieval** step (using IR metrics like hit rate, MRR, NDCG) and the **end-to-end response** (using human feedback or LLM-based evals).

### Level 1: Table-Stakes Techniques
These are foundational optimizations that every developer should consider first.

- **Chunk Size Tuning**: Experiment with different chunk sizes. Smaller, more focused chunks can improve retrieval precision, but there's a tradeoff. More retrieved tokens doesn't always equal better performance.
- **Metadata Filtering**: Add structured metadata (e.g., dates, authors, categories) to your text chunks. Use this to perform a filtered search in the vector database, combining semantic search with precise structured queries (like a `WHERE` clause in SQL) to drastically improve retrieval precision.

### Level 2: Advanced Retrieval Strategies
If basic techniques aren't enough, explore more sophisticated retrieval patterns.

- **Small-to-Big Retrieval**: Embed smaller, more granular chunks (like sentences) to achieve high-precision retrieval. During synthesis, expand the context window by providing the LLM with the larger parent chunk that the retrieved sentence belongs to. This gives the LLM precise context without sacrificing the broader picture.
- **Embedding Alternative Representations**: Instead of embedding the raw text chunk, embed a different representation of it. This could be a **summary of the chunk** or a list of **hypothetical questions** the chunk can answer. This can align the embedded representation more closely with the likely user queries.

### Level 3: Expressive & Powerful Approaches
These are advanced, forward-looking techniques for tackling complex analysis and maximizing performance.

- **Multi-Document Agents**: Move beyond simple Q&A by modeling each document as an **agentic tool**. An agent can then perform complex tasks by retrieving and using tools like `summarize_document` or `query_document_for_facts` across multiple sources, enabling sophisticated reasoning and analysis.

- **Fine-Tuning**: Adapt the models to your specific data and tasks.
  - **Fine-Tune Embeddings**: Fine-tune an embedding model on a synthetically generated dataset of (query, relevant_chunk) pairs from your own data. This specializes the embeddings for your domain, leading to more accurate retrieval.
    > [!TIP]
    > Fine-tuning an adapter on top of the embedding model is often more efficient, as it doesn't require retraining the entire base model or re-indexing your documents if you only adapt the query encoder.
  - **Fine-Tune the LLM**: Use a powerful model (like GPT-4) to generate high-quality example outputs (e.g., with chain-of-thought reasoning) and use this data to fine-tune a smaller, cheaper model (like Llama 2). This process of distillation can teach the smaller model to produce better-structured and higher-quality responses.
transcription:
## Introduction to Production-Ready RAG

Hey everyone, my name is Jerry, co-founder and CEO of LlamaIndex, and today we'll be talking about how to build production-ready RAG applications. I think there's still time for a raffle for the bucket hat, so if you guys stop by our booth, please fill out the Google form. Okay, let's get started.

So what everybody knows is that there's been a ton of amazing use cases in GenAI recently. You know, knowledge search and QA, conversational agents, workflow automation, document processing—these are all things that you can build, especially using the reasoning capabilities of LLMs over your data.

So if we just do a quick refresher in terms of paradigms for how do you actually get language models to understand data that it hasn't been trained over, there's really like two main paradigms. One is retrieval augmentation, where you fix the model and you basically create a data pipeline to put context into the prompt from some data source into the input prompt of the language model. So like a vector database, you know, like unstructured text, SQL database, etc.

The next paradigm here is fine-tuning. How can we bake knowledge into the weights of the network by actually updating the weights of the model itself, some adapter on top of the model, but basically some sort of training process over some new data to actually incorporate knowledge? We'll probably talk a little bit more about retrieval augmentation, but this is just to help you get started and really understanding the mission statement of the company.

## The Basic RAG Stack: Ingestion and Querying

Okay, let's talk about RAG: retrieval-augmented generation. It's become kind of a buzzword recently, but we'll first walk through the current RAG stack for building a QA system. This really consists of two main components: data ingestion as well as data querying, which contains retrieval and synthesis.

If you're just getting started in LlamaIndex, you can basically do this in around five-ish lines of code, so you don't really need to think about it. But if you do want to learn some of the lower-level components—and I do encourage every AI engineer to basically just learn how these components work under the hood—I would encourage you to check out some of our docs to really understand how do you actually do data ingestion and data querying. Like, how do you actually retrieve from a vector database and how do you synthesize that with an LLM?

So that's basically the key stack that's kind of emerging these days for every sort of chatbot, like chat over your PDF, over your unstructured data. A lot of these things are basically using the same principles of how do you actually load data from some data source and actually retrieve and query over it. But I think as developers are actually developing these applications, they're realizing that this isn't quite enough.

## Challenges with Naive RAG

There's certain issues that you're running into that are blockers for actually being able to productionize these applications. And so what are these challenges with naive RAG?

One aspect here is just that the response—and this is the key thing that we're focused on—the response quality is not very good. You run into, for instance, bad retrieval issues. During the retrieval stage from your vector database, if you're not actually returning the relevant chunks from your vector database, you're not going to be able to have the correct context actually put into the LLM. So this includes certain issues like low precision—not all chunks in the retrieve set are relevant. This leads to hallucination, loss-in-the-middle problems, you have a lot of fluff in the returned response. This could mean low recall—like your top-k isn't high enough or basically the set of information that you need to actually answer the question is just not there. And of course, there's other issues too, like outdated information.

And many of you who are building apps these days might be familiar with some key concepts of just why the LLM isn't always guaranteed to give you a correct answer. There's hallucination, irrelevance, toxicity, bias—there's a lot of issues on the LLM side as well.

## A Framework for Optimizing RAG Systems

So what can we do? What can we actually do to try to improve the performance of a retrieval-augmented generation application? And for many of you, you might be running into certain issues, and it really runs the gamut across the entire pipeline. There's stuff you can do on the data. Can we store additional information beyond just the raw text chunks that you're putting in the vector database? Can you optimize that data pipeline somehow, play around with chunk sizes, that type of thing?

Can you optimize the embedding representation itself? A lot of times when you're using a pre-trained embedding model, it's not really optimal for giving you the best performance. There's the retrieval algorithm. You know, the default thing you do is just look up the top-k most similar elements from your vector database to return to the LLM. Many times that's not enough, and what are kind of both simple things you can do as well as hard things?

And there's also synthesis... so can we use LLMs for more than generation? And so basically, you can use the LLM to actually help you with reasoning, as opposed to just pure generation. You can actually use it to try to reason over a given question, can you break it down into simpler questions, route to different data sources, and kind of have a more sophisticated way of querying your data?

## The First Step: How to Evaluate Your RAG System

Of course, like if you've kind of been around some of my recent talks, I always say before you actually try any of these techniques, you need to be pretty task-specific and make sure that you have a way to measure performance. So I'll probably spend like 2 minutes talking about evaluation. Simon, my co-founder, just ran a workshop yesterday on really just how do you evaluate, build a data set, evaluate RAG systems, and help iterate on that. If you missed the workshop, don't worry, we'll have the slides and materials available online so that you can take a look.

At a very high level, in terms of evaluation, it's important because you basically need to define a benchmark for your system to understand how are you going to iterate on and improve it. And there's a few different ways you can try to do evaluation. I think Anton from Chroma was just saying some of this, but you basically need a way to evaluate both the end-to-end solution—like you have your input query as well as the output response—you also want to probably be able to evaluate specific components. Like, if you've diagnosed that the retrieval is the portion that needs improving, you need retrieval metrics to really understand how can you improve your retrieval system.

So there's retrieval and there's synthesis. Let's talk a little bit, just like 30 seconds on each one. Evaluation on retrieval: what does this look like? You basically want to make sure that the stuff that's returned actually answers the query and that you're kind of not returning a bunch of fluff and that the stuff that you return is relevant to the question.

So first, you need an evaluation dataset. A lot of people have human-labeled datasets. If you're building stuff in prod, you might have user feedback as well. If not, you can synthetically generate a dataset. This dataset is input query and output the IDs of the returned documents that are relevant to the query. So you need that somehow. Once you have that, you can measure stuff with ranking metrics, right? You can measure stuff like success rate, hit rate, MRR, NDCG, a variety of these things. And so like once you are able to evaluate this, this really isn't an LLM problem, this is like an IR problem. And this has been around for at least a decade or two, but a lot of this is becoming, you know, it's still very relevant in the face of actually building these LLM apps.

The next piece here is, there's the retrieve portion, but then you generate a response from it, and then how do you actually evaluate the whole thing end-to-end? So evaluation of the final response, given the input, you still want to generate some sort of dataset. So you could do that through human annotations, user feedback, you could have ground truth reference answers given the query that really indicates, hey, this is the proper answer to this question. And you can also just synthetically generate it with GPT-4. You run this through the full RAG pipeline that you built, the retrieval and synthesis, and you can run LLM-based evals. So label-free evals with labeled evals. There's a lot of projects these days going on about how do you actually properly evaluate the predicted outputs of a language model.

## A Tiered Approach to RAG Optimization

Once you've defined your eval benchmark, now you want to think about how do you actually optimize your RAG systems. So I sent a teaser on this slide yesterday, but the way I think about this is that when you want to actually improve your system, there's like a million things that you can do to try to actually improve your RAG system. And you probably don't want to start with the hard stuff first, just because part of the value of language models is how it's kind of democratized access to every developer. It's really just made it easy for people to get up and running.

And so if, for instance, you're running into some performance issues with RAG, I'd probably start with the basics. I call it like table-stakes RAG techniques: better parsing so that you don't just split by even chunks, adjusting your chunk sizes, trying out stuff that's already integrated with a vector database like hybrid search, as well as metadata filters.

There's also advanced retrieval methods that you could try. This is a little bit more advanced. Some of it pulls from traditional IR, some of it is more kind of new in this age of LLM-based apps. There's reranking, that's a traditional concept. There's also concepts in LlamaIndex like recursive retrieval, dealing with embedded tables, small-to-big retrieval, and a lot of other stuff that we have that help you potentially improve the performance of your application.

And then the last bit, this kind of gets into more expressive stuff that might be harder to implement, might incur a higher latency and cost, but is potentially more powerful and forward-looking, is like agents. How do you incorporate agents towards better RAG pipelines to better answer different types of questions and synthesize information? And how do you actually fine-tune stuff?

## Table-Stakes #1: Tuning Chunk Size

Let's talk a little bit about the table stakes first. So chunk sizes: tuning your chunk size can have outsize impacts on performance, right? If you've kind of played around with RAG systems, this may or may not be obvious to you. What's interesting though is that like more retrieved tokens does not always equate to higher performance. And that if you do reranking of your retrieved tokens, it doesn't necessarily mean that your final generation response is going to be better. And this is again due to stuff like lost-in-the-middle problems, where stuff in the middle of the LLM context window tends to get lost, whereas stuff at the end tends to be a little bit more well-remembered by the LLM.

And so I think we did a workshop with Arize a few weeks ago where basically we showed, you know, there is kind of an optimal chunk size given your dataset. And a lot of times when you try out stuff like reranking, it actually increases your error metrics.

## Table-Stakes #2: Metadata Filtering

Metadata filtering. This is another very table-stakes thing that I think everybody should look into. And I think vector databases like Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate—these vector databases are all implementing these capabilities under the hood. Metadata filtering is basically just like, how can you add structured context to your text chunks? And you can use this for both embeddings as well as synthesis, but it also integrates with the metadata filter capabilities of a vector database.

So metadata is just like, again, structured JSON dictionary. It could be like page number, it could be the document title, it could be the summary of adjacent chunks. You can get creative with it too. You could hallucinate questions that the chunk answers, and it can help retrieval, it can help augment your response quality. It also integrates with the vector database filters.

So as an example, let's say the question is over the SEC 10-Q document, and it's like, "Can you tell me the risk factors in 2021?" If you just do raw semantic search, typically it's very low precision. You're going to return a bunch of stuff that may or may not match this. You might even return stuff from other years if you have a bunch of documents from different years in the same vector collection. And so you're kind of rolling the dice a little bit.

But one idea here is basically, you know, if you have access to the metadata of the documents and you ask a question like this, you basically combine structured query capabilities by inferring the metadata filters—like a WHERE clause in a SQL statement, like year equals 2021—and you combine that with semantic search to return the most relevant candidates given your query. And this improves the precision of your results.

## Advanced Retrieval: Small-to-Big and Reference Embedding

Moving on to stuff that's maybe a bit more advanced, like advanced retrieval. One thing that we found generally helps is this idea of like small-to-big retrieval. So what does that mean? Basically, right now when you embed a big text chunk, you also synthesize over that text chunk, and so it's a little suboptimal. Because what if the embedding representation's biased because there's a bunch of fluff in that text chunk that contains a bunch of irrelevant information? You're not actually optimizing your retrieval quality. So embedding a big text chunk sometimes feels a little suboptimal.

One thing that you could do is basically embed text at the sentence level or on a smaller level and then expand that window during synthesis time. And so this is contained in a variety of LlamaIndex abstractions, but the idea is that you retrieve on more granular pieces of information, so smaller chunks. This makes it so that these chunks are more likely to be retrieved when you actually ask a query over these specific pieces of context. But then you want to make sure that the LLM actually has access to more information to actually synthesize a proper result. So this leads to more precise retrieval, right? So we tried this out, it helps avoid some loss-in-the-middle problems. You can set a smaller top-k value, like k=2, whereas over this dataset, if you set k=5 for naive retrieval over big text chunks, you basically start returning a lot of context and that kind of leads into issues where, you know, maybe the relevant context is in the middle but you're not able to find out, or the LLM is not able to kind of synthesize over that information.

A very related idea here is just like embedding a reference to the parent chunk, as opposed to the actual text chunk itself. So for instance, if you want to embed not just the raw text chunk, or not the text chunk but actually like a smaller chunk, or a summary, or questions that answer the chunk, we have found that that actually helps to improve retrieval performance a decent amount. And it kind of again goes along with this idea: a lot of times you want to embed something that's more amenable for embedding-based retrieval, but then you want to return enough context so that the LLM can actually synthesize over that information.

## Using Agents for More Sophisticated Analysis

The next bit here is actually kind of even more advanced stuff. This goes on into agents and this goes on into that last pillar that I mentioned, which is how can you use LLMs for reasoning as opposed to just synthesis?

The intuition here is that for a lot of RAG, if you're just using the LLM at the end, you're one, constrained by the quality of your retriever, and you're really only able to do stuff like question answering. And there's certain types of questions and more advanced analysis that you might want to launch that top-k RAG can't really answer. It's not necessarily just a one-off question. You might need to have an entire sequence of reasoning steps to actually pull together a piece of information, or you might want to summarize a document and compare with other documents.

So one kind of architecture we're exploring right now is this idea of multi-document agents. What if instead of just RAG, we moved a little bit more into agent territory? We modeled each document not just as a sequence of text chunks, but actually as a set of tools that contains the ability to both summarize that document as well as to do QA over that document over specific facts. And of course, if you want to scale to hundreds or thousands or millions of documents, typically an agent can only have access to a limited window of tools. So you probably want to do some sort of retrieval on these tools, similar to how you want to retrieve text chunks from a document. The main difference is that because these are tools, you actually want to act upon them. You want to use them as opposed to just taking the raw text and plugging it into the context window. So blending this combination of embedding-based retrieval or any sort of retrieval as well as agent tool use is a very interesting paradigm that I think is really only possible with this age of LLMs and hasn't really existed before.

## Advanced Technique: Fine-Tuning Embeddings and LLMs

This another kind of advanced concept is this idea of fine-tuning. And so fine-tuning, you know, some other presenters have talked about this as well, but the idea of fine-tuning in a RAG system is that it really optimizes specific pieces of this RAG pipeline for you to kind of better improve the performance of either retriever or synthesis capabilities.

So one thing you can do is fine-tune your embeddings. I think Anton was talking about this as well. Like if you just use a pre-trained model, the embedding representations are not going to be optimized over your specific data. So sometimes you're just going to retrieve the wrong information. If you can somehow tune these embeddings so that given any sort of relevant question that the user might ask, that you're actually returning the relevant response, then you're going to have better performance.

So an idea here is to generate a synthetic query dataset from raw text chunks using LLMs and use this to fine-tune an embedding model. And you can do this by basically fine-tuning the base model itself, you can also fine-tune an adapter on top of the model. And fine-tuning an adapter on top of the model has a few advantages in that you don't require the base model's weights to actually fine-tune stuff, and if you just fine-tune the query, you don't have to re-index your entire document corpus.

There's also fine-tuning LLMs, which of course a lot of people are very interested in doing these days. And the intuition here specifically for RAG is that if you have a weaker LLM like 3.5 Turbo, Llama 2 7B, these weaker LLMs are not bad at... weaker LLMs are maybe a little bit worse at response synthesis, reasoning, structured outputs, etc., compared to bigger models. So the solution here is, what if you can generate a synthetic dataset using a bigger model like GPT-4 that we're exploring, and you actually distill that into 3.5 Turbo so it gets better at chain-of-thought, longer response quality, better structured outputs, and a lot of other possibilities as well.

So all these things are in our docs. There's production RAG, there's fine-tuning, and I have two seconds left. So thank you very much.
